ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, an elastic bumper is installed at the bottom of a fixed inclined plane with an inclination angle of $\theta$. The masses of two blocks, P and Q, are $m$ and $4m$, respectively. Q is initially at rest at point A on the inclined plane. At a certain moment, P collides elastically with Q with an upward velocity $v_{0}$ along the inclined plane. The coefficient of kinetic friction between Q and the inclined plane is equal to $\tan \theta$, and the maximum static friction is equal to the sliding friction. There is no friction between P and the inclined plane, and there is no loss of kinetic energy in the collision between P and the bumper. Both blocks can be considered as point masses. The inclined plane is sufficiently long, and P will not collide with Q before Q's velocity reduces to zero. The magnitude of gravitational acceleration is $g$.

1. Determine the magnitudes of the velocities of P and Q, $v_{P_{1}}$ and $v_{Q_{1}}$, immediately after the first collision between P and Q.
2. Determine the height $h_{n}$ that block Q rises to after the $n$-th collision.
3. Determine the total height $H$ that block Q rises from point A.
4. To ensure that P does not collide with Q before Q's velocity reduces to zero, determine the minimum distance $s$ between point A and the bumper.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
The speed of P is $\frac{3}{5}v_{0}$, The speed of Q is$\frac{2}{5}v_{0}$
$h_{n}=(\frac{7}{25})^{n-1}\cdot\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{25g}$ ($n=1,2,3 \ldots$)
$H=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{18g}$
$s=\frac{(8\sqrt{7}-13)v_{0}^{2}}{200g\sin\theta}$

Two small blocks P and Q are located near A on the inclined plane, P is on the lower-left side, Q is on the upper-right side and they are in contact; the arrow v0 is along the inclined plane upward to the right, indicating that P collides with Q with a velocity up along the inclined plane. Reasoning: take upward along the inclined plane as positive, and denote a = g sinθ. P has no friction with the inclined plane, so on the inclined plane P is subject only to the component of gravity along the inclined plane, whose magnitude corresponds to acceleration a, directed down along the inclined plane. Between Q and the inclined plane μ = tanθ, so when Q slides upward, the friction force is down along the inclined plane, with magnitude μ·4mg cosθ = 4mg sinθ; the component of gravity along the inclined plane is also 4mg sinθ, so the deceleration of Q when sliding upward is 2g sinθ = 2a. After Q comes to rest, the maximum static friction force also equals 4mg sinθ, just able to balance the component of gravity along the inclined plane, so Q can stop in place and wait for the next collision. 1. First collision: P has mass m, Q has mass 4m, Q's initial speed is 0, and P's initial speed is v0. According to the one-dimensional elastic collision formula, P's velocity after collision is v_P1 = [(m - 4m)/(m + 4m)]v0 = -3v0/5, and Q's velocity after collision is v_Q1 = [2m/(m + 4m)]v0 = 2v0/5. Therefore the speed magnitudes are respectively 3v0/5 and 2v0/5. 2. The nth collision: suppose before the nth collision, P's velocity up along the inclined plane is V_n, and Q has already come to rest. After the elastic collision, P's velocity magnitude down along the inclined plane is 3V_n/5, and Q's velocity up along the inclined plane is 2V_n/5. Q slides upward with deceleration 2a, so its upward distance along the inclined plane is [(2V_n/5)^2]/(2·2a) = V_n^2/(25a). The corresponding vertical height is h_n = [V_n^2/(25a)]sinθ = V_n^2/(25g). After the collision, P first slides down to the baffle and rebounds, with no mechanical energy loss. When it climbs from the position of the nth collision to Q's new rest position, it needs to increase vertical height h_n, so the speed before the n+1th collision satisfies V_{n+1}^2 = (3V_n/5)^2 - 2g h_n = 9V_n^2/25 - 2V_n^2/25 = 7V_n^2/25. Also V_1 = v0, so V_n^2 = (7/25)^(n-1)v0^2. Thus h_n = (7/25)^(n-1) v0^2/(25g). 3. The total rising height of Q from point A is the sum of all h_n: H = Σ h_n = [v0^2/(25g)]/[1 - 7/25] = v0^2/(18g). 4. Find the minimum distance s from A to the baffle. The constraint condition takes equality in the first round: P just reaches Q's stopping position at the instant Q stops. After the first collision, P's velocity magnitude down along the inclined plane from point A is 3v0/5. Suppose its velocity before reaching the baffle is w, then w^2 = (3v0/5)^2 + 2as. Q's velocity after the first collision is 2v0/5, and its deceleration is 2a, so the stopping time t_Q = (2v0/5)/(2a) = v0/(5a). The time for P to slide down to the baffle is [w - 3v0/5]/a. After rebounding from the baffle, P goes upward to Q's new stopping position, and its velocity for this upward segment from the previous recurrence result is sqrt(7)v0/5, so the time for this upward segment is [w - sqrt(7)v0/5]/a. The critical condition is that P's total round-trip time equals Q's stopping time: {[w - 3v0/5] + [w - sqrt(7)v0/5]}/a = v0/(5a). Solving gives 2w = (4 + sqrt(7))v0/5, that is w = (4 + sqrt(7))v0/10. Substituting into w^2 = (3v0/5)^2 + 2as gives 2as = [(4 + sqrt(7))^2/100 - 9/25]v0^2 = (8sqrt(7) - 13)v0^2/100, so s = (8sqrt(7) - 13)v0^2/(200g sinθ). In subsequent rounds, V_n decreases by a geometric factor, while Q's position relative to the baffle is already farther, so the constraint is not stronger than in the first round.
